body: At your scale, ratio beats reach. A post that reaches 120 people and moves 40 of them is doing more work than one that reaches 300 and moves 15.
Your all-time benchmark is the EP announcement: 185 engagement on 112 reach — a 1.65 ratio. Anything above 0.5 is a genuinely strong post for this account.
Reach between 100 and 250 is your normal. Don't read a 140-reach post as a failure — read what the people who saw it did.
Saves are the quiet superstar metric. A post with 10 saves and 20 likes beat a post with 60 likes and none — saves predict who'll come back.
Shares are the loudest signal Instagram hears. Every share is a fan doing your promotion for you — one share is worth roughly four likes to the ranking system.
Comments count double when you answer them. The reply thread is engagement the algorithm attributes to the post — a conversation is worth more than its comment count.
A Reel's first hour is a cold-audience audition. Strong early watch-through widens distribution; a slow first hour usually means the hook, not the song.
When a personal post out-reaches a promo post — and it will — that's not noise. 'New hair ✂️' hit 241 reach on three words. The account rewards the human.
Read stats in batches of five posts, not one at a time. One post is weather; five posts are climate. Change strategy on climate.
If reach spiked but engagement didn't, non-followers saw it and scrolled past. The hook worked; the content didn't hold. If both spiked, you found a repeatable format.
Older posts (pre-2023) may show no metrics at all — Instagram doesn't provide insights for media posted before the account became a business account. It's a data gap, not a bad post.
Views on a Reel mean less than watch-through. 400 views at 3 seconds each is a weak hook; 150 views where people finish is a post to make again.
Carousels report engagement across all slides — a strong carousel often shows modest likes but heavy saves. Judge carousels on saves first.
Posting time shows up in the first-hour numbers. Same content type, two different windows, three tries each — that's a real experiment; anything less is a hunch.
Your top posts share a fingerprint: real moment, real names, gratitude or humor, zero polish. When a new post scores high, check it against that fingerprint before crediting the topic.
Engagement rate above 3% of reach is healthy at any size. Your best posts run far past that — which means your ceiling is a content problem, never an audience-size problem.
A cover song that outperforms your originals isn't an insult — it's a door. The familiarity got the reach; note how many stayed to check who you are.
Zero-comment posts aren't dead if saves and shares moved. Some formats are savers, not talkers — a lyric sheet gets bookmarked, not discussed.
Follower count is the vanity metric at this stage; reach-per-post is the real one. 2,900 followers who see and share beats 10,000 who don't.
If a show-announcement post underperforms, the show isn't in trouble — announcements are utility posts. Judge them on Event RSVPs and Story link taps, not likes.
One outlier post doesn't make a strategy. Two posts with the same shape both outperforming — that's a format. Three is a franchise. Count to three before you commit.
Reels reach non-followers; Feed posts feed the faithful. Low Reel engagement with decent reach means new eyes — that's the format doing its actual job.
The ratio on a post climbs for about 48 hours, then fossilizes. Read stats on Thursday for Tuesday's post — day-of numbers always undersell it.
When engagement is all likes and nothing else, the post was agreeable but not useful. Likes are applause; saves and shares are requests for more.
Facebook numbers will read smaller and older — fewer reactions, more event responses and comments from people you know. That's the platform working, not failing.
A sudden reach dip across several posts in a row is usually seasonal or platform-wide, not you. Check whether the ratio held — if it did, your audience didn't go anywhere.
Story views tell you your true regulars: the same 40–60 people tapping through daily is a core fanbase most small artists can't see. They're the ones who buy tickets.
Judge a post against its own format's average, not the account average. Your Reels, carousels, and photos live in three different economies.
The posts you almost didn't publish — too rough, too small — routinely land in your top quartile. When one does, believe the data over the doubt; rough is the brand.
High reach on a collab post partly belongs to the collaborator's audience. Compare it to your solo posts separately, or every solo post will look like a letdown.
If the same three fans carry every comment section, that's not a small audience problem — that's a visible superfan layer. Name-check them occasionally; superfans multiply when noticed.
An engagement spike with no reach spike means your existing fans loved it. That's the post to make a series from — the algorithm eventually follows the fans.
Watch what the top comment is. When it's a question, your next post is the answer — pre-validated content with a built-in first commenter.
Late-evening posts for new-release and BTS content is a music-specific pattern in the data — arts audiences scroll after the day ends. Test 8–10pm MT for release-adjacent posts.
Reach on a FEED photo decays in a day; a Reel can resurface for weeks. A Reel's fourth-week numbers are real — check back before you call one a miss.
Don't compare your numbers to accounts with 50K followers — under that line the algorithm scores engagement quality over audience size, which is exactly the game you can win.
If saves are climbing account-wide quarter over quarter, your utility content is compounding. That trend line matters more than any single post's spike.
A post that took two hours and one that took two minutes will often score the same here. Track effort against ratio for a month — let the data set your production budget.
Shares on a show announcement are RSVPs in disguise — each one is a fan telling a specific friend 'we're going.' Weight them over likes when reading promo posts.
The engagement on your gratitude posts isn't politeness — thank-you posts with real names tagged consistently outperform. Tagged people share, and their audiences follow the tag.
Metrics can't hear the songs. A quiet post that sold two tickets or one merch order out-earned a loud one that sold none — close the loop with what actually happened at the show.
When a format stops working — and every format eventually does — the data shows it as three straight below-average posts of the same shape. Retire it for a season, not forever.
